extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators and students of classical rhetoric / public speaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and delivering forensic and public orations in the classical rhetorical tradition, covering requisite knowledge, structure, stylistic figures, pacing, and adaptation to audience and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of manner and style
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator should frequently vary his manner of speaking — not always maintain the highest energy of language but sometimes descend to the style of conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: poets and actors vary their styles; Demosthenes alternates simplicity, nervousness, and mixed character in different orations. Avoid delivering every cause in the same strain; adapt tone to character, audience, and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of Logic (reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The finished orator should make himself master of everything in the art of Logic applicable to his profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know forces, extensions and species of words; modes of expressing conceptions; how to distinguish true from false propositions; infer consequences from premises; identify opposites; resolve ambiguities by accurate distinction. Logic supplies the material of sound reasoning even in oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to define and divide subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Settle clearly what is to be discoursed upon by providing definitions and dividing the genus into its proper species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should be explicit and copious (adapted to common understanding), not the contracted forms of academic debates. Division should avoid defect or redundancy and permit proper distribution of the discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of moral topics (materials of eloquence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be acquainted with common and useful branches of morality to speak with spirit, dignity, and freedom on topics like religion, death, filial piety, love of country, virtues and vices, grief and pleasure, and other emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These form the ‘materials’ of Eloquence: a plentiful stock of sentiments (suitable for both learned and vulgar audiences) supplies content before considering language and manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with Natural Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquaintance with principles of Natural Philosophy elevates thought and speech, giving a more dignified and splendid manner when treating lofty subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of higher contemplations helps an orator descend to human concerns with greater dignity and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of Civil Law and Jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator should make himself master of the Civil Law, equity, and jurisprudential principles necessary for judicial causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is scandalous to plead without proper knowledge of laws; legal knowledge is of daily necessity in forensic causes and enables accurate handling of points of law and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with history and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Be well versed in history and venerable records of antiquity (especially of one's own country) to produce pertinent and striking examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples add dignity and weight; knowledge of past events connects a mortal's life to ancestors and instructs the audience. Use striking examples to enliven and enforce arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand types of judicial controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that judicial controversy turns either upon matter of fact or on the meaning/expression of words; facts may concern reality, equity, or legal name; expressions may be ambiguous or contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity often arises when spirit and letter of law conflict; identifying the kind of cause narrows the rules for invention and treatment of arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention of arguments (topics/commonplaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive arguments from commonplaces (topics) that are either inherent in the subject or assumptive; skillful use of inherent topics gives weight to discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because kinds of causes are few, rules for invention must be few. Inherent topics are easy and familiar to the understanding and often most effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and parts of an oration
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage the parts: begin to conciliate good-will/raise expectation/prepare the audience; state the case concisely and plausibly; support proofs and refute opponents in an orderly manner; conclude with a peroration to inflame or allay passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part (introduction, narration, proof, refutation, peroration) must be conducted appropriately to the occasion; they are intricate and vary by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion and adaptation to time and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence requires discretion — a perfect mastery of time and character — so the orator adapts language and manner to occasion, audience, opponent, judge, and subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not speak in the same invariable manner on every occasion. Proportion language: modest introductions, conversational narratives, expanded language for dignified subjects, restrained treatment for slight causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of ornament (amplification and thesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamentation chiefly serves two occasions: discussion of indefinite questions or general truths (thesis) and amplification/exaggeration (auxesis); commonplaces are also fertile ground for ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ornament more or less through discourse but especially in amplifying general propositions or commonplaces; apply general sentiments to particular cases to allow mitigation or severity as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of manner (ethic) and pathos (pathetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine a propriety of manner (mild, insinuating, conciliatory) with the pathetic (energetic, passion-rousing) as appropriate; both are essential sources of Eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ethic adapts to dispositions and stations of life; the pathetic rouses passions and can seize a cause by force. Use mildness to conciliate, force to overwhelm when occasion demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic emotional engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker must genuinely feel the ardor he wishes to convey; passion in the speaker is necessary to inflame the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No language will inflame unless the speaker himself glows with importance of subject. Examples: gestures, dramatic acts (lifting an infant), and real concern enhance effect (Cicero's own examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of language (formal rhetorical figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ figures of language to embellish and surprise: doubling/repetition, slight variation, beginning/ending sentences similarly, using same word to end one and begin next, repeating a word with different meaning, corresponding words, contrasting opposites, gradation, ellipsis (dropping conjunctives), aposiopesis (sudden breaking off), feigned correction, exclamation, varied cases of a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures of language are like theatrical decorations — they embellish and surprise. Use them to create agreeable sound and ornament, but regulate them by skillful disposition of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of sentiment (devices of thought and feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use figures of sentiment: exhibit an idea in different points of view; dwell on a good argument; extenuate unfavorable points; use raillery; feign deviation; announce principal points; summarize force of arguments; check or reiterate ardent expressions; close paragraphs with weighty sentiment; press adversary by repeated questions; reason with oneself; use irony, feigned doubt, division of action, feigned omission, appeals, imitation of persons, personification, and occasional descent to familiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the life of popular eloquence; they enable amplification, diversion, preemption of objections, and emotional manipulation. The text lists many examples and permutations — apply them judiciously and variedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other stylistic beauties (brevity, pathos, humour, imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue brevity where required; lively and pathetic description of occurrences; passionate exaggeration of remarkable circumstances; earnestness implying more than is said; well-timed variety of humour; imitation of different characters and dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance brevity and expansion according to subject. Variety of humour and faithful imitation enrich delivery and maintain audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper formation and regulation of figures by word arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, however numerous, must be properly formed and regulated by a skilful disposition of their constituent words to attain the merit required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures alone do not suffice; their efficacy depends on precise arrangement and harmony of words (to be treated in subsequent sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concinnity and agreeable connection of words (prosaic harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange words so each following one is aptly connected to the preceding, producing agreeable sound, measured cadence, and concinnity of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to structure without laborious nicety; avoid chasms or harshness that offend the ear. The mind and ear should readily discern natural connections; practice habituates one to necessary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euphony: avoid vowel collisions and use contraction for sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid collisions of vowels (where adjacent vowels produce harshness); use contraction and abbreviation of words and names for smoother and more agreeable sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romans avoid vowel collisions; poets sometimes admit breaks for metre. Contractions (e.g. multi' modis, palm' et crinibus) and abbreviated names (Duellum→Bellum) are used for euphony and brevity.
